thread.title: Did the Federal Reserve Trigger the FAANG Slide?

author: Randall W. Forsyth
title: Did the Federal Reserve Trigger the FAANG Slide?
text:
Illustration: See-ming Lee Updated Aug. 1, 2018 10:20 a.m. ET Money makes the mare go, according to old English proverb, but more importantly, money makes the markets go. And it’s far from an original observation that the money created through the securities purchases by the Federal Reserve and other central banks has inflated the value of risk assets such as stocks, which, after all, was the aim of so-called quantitative easing .
Now, as the Fed begins to shrink its balance sheet, George Goncalves, the head of rates strategy at Nomura Securities, observes the connection is less obvious. But during weeks in which the Fed markedly reduces its holdings of Treasuries and agency mortgage-backed securities , or MBS, the stock market has a rocky time.
This week, moreover, is one of them. But don’t jump to blaming the Fed for the slide in the FAANG stocks— Facebook (FB), Apple (AAPL), Amazon.com (AMZN), Netflix (NFLX), and Google parent Alphabet (GOOGL)—just yet.
Goncalves notes in a research report that the connection between the Fed’s balance sheet and the S&P 500 has become less precise since the central bank has begun to shed assets. While the Fed’s balance sheet has shrunk $200 billion from its peak of $4.5 trillion, the S&P 500’s market value has increased over $2 trillion.
To be sure, the Fed’s shrinkage has been offset by the inflation in other central banks’ purchases, notably that of the European Central Bank and the Bank of Japan. “That plus financial engineering (stock buybacks) have eased the drag of QT,” or quantitative tightening, he adds.
Notwithstanding the claim by former Fed Chair Janet Yellen that winding down the central bank’s portfolio should be like watching paint dry , it’s actually been a bit more exciting, albeit only sporadically.
The process proceeds in “big chunks,” Goncalves observes. In practice, the Fed shrinks its holdings by letting a certain amount of Treasuries and MBS mature. Starting July 1, the Fed is rolling over maturing Treasuries only in excess of stated caps of $24 billion coming due, and $16 billion of MBS coming due.
Treasury and mortgage securities don’t get paid down in a steady, linear fashion every day but in lumps, he points out. As it happened, one of those big redemption weeks came just before the big surge in volatility and swoon in stocks during the week ended Feb. 7. That was when the Cboe Volatility Index, or VIX—the equity market’s so-called fear gauge—spiked, which set off a chain reaction that saw the S&P 500 plunge over 5% .
As it happens, the Fed’s holdings of Treasury securities will decline by $24 billion in the week ending Wednesday. And as you may have noticed, the Nasdaq Composite has been a bit wobbly the past few days, most notably in the FAANG stocks. Any connection?
In an email, Goncalves avers that the biggest market impacts come when there are big rolloffs of both Treasuries and mortgage securities, but he isn’t prepared to connect the gyrations of technology stocks to the Fed’s portfolios. Still, as the central bank pares its balance sheet at an increasing pace, those weeks of big redemptions will become more common.
Circle on your calendar the week ending on Halloween, Oct. 31, when $23.8 billion in Treasuries and $9.4 billion of mortgages will be paid down, according to Nomura’s projections. In the week ending Nov. 21, $17.4 billion of Treasuries will run off while $9.6 billion of mortgages will be redeemed. And next year will see those big redemption weeks coming around lots more frequently.
Market participants scrutinize intently the Fed’s words and deeds when it comes to its interest rate policy. The results of the meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee that will wind up Wednesday will be no different. But what goes on behind the scenes with the central bank’s securities portfolio may be at least as important.
Corrections & Amplifications
In the week ending Oct. 31, 2018, the Federal Reserve will pay down $23.8 billion in Treasuries. An earlier version of this column mistakenly gave the amount as $423.8 billion.
